In that version, two fishermen catch a giant fish, but they are unable to pull him out of the water. They cut off his head, but then they regret their actions, as the giant's blood forms a new head. This process is repeated three times, until the two fishermen give up and let the giant go.

Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". They escaped to the shore, and hid behind a log. My relatives do not know where I have gone. But you," he said, turning to the other, "may go with them." So one of the young men went, but the other returned home. And the warriors went on up the river to a town on the other side of Kalama. The people came down to the water and they began to fight, and many were killed. But presently the young man heard one of the warriors say, "Quick, let us go home: that man has been hit." Now he thought: "Oh, they are ghosts." He did not feel sick, but they said he had been shot. So the canoes went back to Egulac and the young man went ashore to his house and made a fire. And he told everybody and said: "Behold I accompanied the ghosts, and we went to fight. When the sun rose he fell down. Something black came out of his mouth. His face became contorted. The people jumped up and cried. He was dead.

Explanation
This is the start of a story told by the Tlingit people. The full story, told in Ravenna Tlingit, is as follows:
One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then the water rose and the men were separated. One of them was taken by a seal and the other one returned to the village. He told the people of Egulac that he and his companion had been taken by a seal and that he alone had returned. From that day on he was known as "the one who escaped". His companion, "the one who was taken", was gone forever.
This story is told to explain the origin of the name "Egulac", which is also the name of a Tlingit community on Admiralty Island in Southeast Alaska. The community was formerly known as "Baasco Daak'ił", "the place where canoes are tied up".

The story has been interpreted as a creation story, explaining how bears came to be.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then the water rose, the tide came in, and the two men were left on an island of grass. Their fire went out, and they could not find another match. One of the men took off his belt and wrapped it around the other man's neck and said, "Now, my friend, you are an islander, and I am the mainlander. If I should die, do not cry for me."  Then he pushed the other man off the island and went back to the mainland.
The man on the island screamed all night, but no one heard him. The next morning he was gone.
From that day on, the current was too strong for the canoes to cross. But the natives, they said, could swim to the island when the tide was going out.  And they explained that the island was really a giant clam shell, and that the man had been trapped and killed by the rising tide.

So the two young men helped the whale, and the whale helped them, and they lived happily ever after. And every time they went down to the seashore to hunt seals, they would sing a song and the whale would come and they would laugh and talk and sing.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then the wind came up and the waves were so high that the two young men were separated. One of them was taken by the people from the other side and when he was brought before the chief, he was put in jail. The other young man came to the mission and he was very sad and worried about his brother. He asked the priest if he could help him get his brother released. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The priest could not do it because he was not the chief. He advised the young man to go to the chief and ask him to release his brother.
The young man went to the chief and explained the situation. The chief was angry and said that the other side had sent a message saying that they would keep the young man's brother as long as he was alive. The chief then ordered his men to prepare for war.
The young man was scared and he ran away. He went to the mission and he told the priest what had happened. The priest then sent a message to the other side saying that the war was unnecessary because he would convince the young man to go back and hunt seals again.
When the young men returned, the chief was happy and he ordered his men to make peace. From that day on, the two sides lived in peace and the young men were known as "The Two Heroes of Egulac."

[Edit] The story behind the story
This story was popular among the Tlingit people. It was told by Chris Wilson, a Tlingit from Juneau, to his son, Frank, in 1964. The story has been recorded in writing since at least 1901, when it was translated from Tlingit to English by Marie K. Reappah.

Biography

He was awarded a Distinguished Service Order and made a Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George. He died in 1970.

Interpretation
This is a story from the Eskimo, or Inuit, people. It is similar to other stories from this culture in that it uses the imagery of seals and the sea to describe events. The two men are stranded on an island, and they wait for morning to come. When it does, one of the men kills a seagull, possibly as food, possibly as a sacrifice. The story does not explain why the men were on the island in the first place, or why one of them had to die. It is simply a description of what happened, without any explanation or judgment.

One Night Two Men from Egulac is a work of fiction by Canadian author Timothy Kim. It was first published in 1990 by House of Anansi Press. The novel tells the story of two young men from the Nuu-chah-nulth tribe who go down to the river to hunt seals. One night, as they are returning home, they are caught in a great storm. One of the men is blown away by the wind. The other man, Nootka, saves himself by holding on to the ropes of his boat. He rows back to the village and tells the people what has happened. A search party is organized and the missing man is found on an island. He has been there for four years and has gone mad. He is taken back to the village, but he is unable to speak. The novel explores themes of nature, time, and the human spirit.

There are several variants of this story, and they all center on the idea of a supernatural canoe race. Canoe race
Every year, the Siksika hold a "Half Moon" canoe race. This race is significant because it is said to be the only time that the canoes are allowed to race against each other. Usually, the canoes work together to hunt, fish, and transport people, and they are not allowed to compete with each other. During the "Half Moon" race, however, the canoes are allowed to compete, and this competition is said to be a time of great excitement and danger.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then the water rose, the tide came in, and the two men were left on an island of grass. Their fire went out, and they could not find another match. One of them lay down and went to sleep, while the other went along the shore, searching for a way to get to the mainland. He looked for a long time, but the fog was so thick that he could not see a thing. Just as he was beginning to lose hope, he heard a voice, "Kiche, Kiche, come over here." It was a woman's voice, and when he went to her, she took him by the hand and led him to a canoe, which was hidden in the long grass. In the morning, when the two friends awoke, one was glad and the other sad. The one who had gone to search for a way to the mainland said, "I went to the edge of the water, and there I saw a canoe hidden in the long grass. I went to the woman who was paddling, and she took me to her people, and they are very wealthy. They wear copper pendants and their canoes are made of the bones of sharks. The woman told me that her people were the only ones who could make fire, and she gave me a match. I have become very rich, and that is why I am glad." The other man was sad, and he said "All I have to offer you is a stone," and he threw a stone into the fire. Suddenly, the fire jumped up, and one flame touched the man's face. Then he, too, was rich. From that day on, whenever those two friends met, one was rich and the other poor, and they lived on the opposite shores of a great river.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then the thunder blew off in the distance. One of the men said to the other, "I do not think the fog and the calm spell good luck. I do not think it at all. The mist is coming up towards us."

As they went on through the fog, one of them kept calling out, "What is that?" And the other kept answering, "I do not know; but it is not a good sign." Soon they heard a voice, "Hello, how are you?" They could not see a thing. They heard the voice again, "Hello, how are you?"

Then they said to one another, "Do you know who that is?"

The other one said, "It is not a good sign. We never heard of anyone asking directions in this river before."

A third time they heard the voice, "Hello, how are you?" And then it came nearer and nearer.

One of the two men said, "I know who it is. It is the spirit of the mist."

At that the other man became very afraid and he said, "Let us go back the way we came."

But the spirit of the mist said, "I mean you no harm. I have been watching you for a long time, and I want to help you. You are the first humans who have ever come here to hunt seals. We will make a deal. You will give me your names and I will tell you where the seals are."

The two men said, "What do we have to do to make a deal?"

The spirit of the mist said, "All I ask is that you tell no one of this. You must not even tell your own people. Go now and tell no one."

Then the two men went back to their village and they told no one.

One night two young Hunkpapa Sioux Indians, Minthy and Tippton, were out from the agency, playing bear meatball (similar to lacrosse) on the upper end of the Grand River. They heard screams, and then saw a large white man walking towards them, carrying a long sharp-pointed stick with a burning brand at the end. The two Indians hid behind a log and watched the white man, who they knew was called Captain Smith.

Smith was calling out to the people in the surrounding woods, "Come out or I will burn you out!" He was the commanding officer of the post at Fort Pitt, and he was determined to catch the "bears" who had stolen a large quantity of bear meat from a trap near the agency.
One of the Indians whispered, "That white devil is crazy."
"Maybe so," said the other. "But he is our friend, and we must help him."
They crept out from behind the log and approached Smith. "Give us the stick, brother," said Minthy. "We will hunt the bears for you."
Smith gave them the stick and went back to the fort. The Indians hid the stick in the hollow of a tree near the river, and then they set off in single file, following the trail of the bears.
For two days they followed the bears, through thickets and over hills. Finally, they came to a strange place where the bears had made a Den. The Indians crept up to the Den, taking care not to make a sound. They saw two large bears inside the Den, and they saw something else.
"Look," whispered Tippton. "They have white men's clothes."
They were right. The bears had on white men's coats, shirts, and trousers. And on the opposite wall of the Den, they saw something that made them even more afraid. It was a picture of a white man, holding a burning brand.

When they returned to the place where they had made their bed, Kakontak said, "I think I should have killed him." 
"Why?" asked the other.
"Because," said Kakontak, "he is from a rich village and he will live a long time."
That night at the chief's potlatch, Kaxoltak stood up and spoke. "I am Kaxoltak," he said. "I am from Kaxoltak. We are allies. We will sing and dance and make merry." 
The people knew that Kakontak was cunning and Kaxoltak was strong. But Kakontak was sly and soon the villagers were whispering that Kaxoltak was the one who had killed the seal. 
"Kill him!" cried the people. But Kaxoltak stood among them and sang a mighty song. He told them of the time long ago when the first Kaxoltak, their ancestor, came among them and brought them under the protection of the great bear.
Then Kaxoltak said, "I am the reincarnation of that first Kaxoltak. I can do all that he could do." 
He stood straight and tall and the people were silent. He had spoken in the name of the Great Bear. From that day on, Kaxoltak was chief.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt for ducks. It was wintertime, and underneath the ice floes great dollies of geese and ducks were trapped by the Edmonton River. The two young men had taken several ducks and were on their way home, carrying their ducks and their guns when they were caught by a group of Cree who were watching these ducks as part of their territory.

The Cree stopped them and demanded to know where they got those ducks. The two young men said "We got them from down river; from over here." "No," said the Cree, "you went to our place. You're stealing our ducks." They argued about it, and finally the Cree threw one of the young men into the river and we went back to their camp with the guns and the ducks. And that was the beginning of it.
The Cree were determined to drive the Blackfoot from this land and keep the ducks for themselves.

This incident sparked a major conflict between the Cree and the Blackfoot. The Blackfoot sent word to the Kootenai to come and help them, and the Kootenai sent White Fish and led a large war party up the river. When the war parties met, there was a great battle on the frozen river. However, the Cree had set ambushes and managed to capture a large number of the Kootenai and Blackfoot. After a lengthy bargaining session, the Cree released their prisoners in exchange for provisions and clothing.
From then on, the Cree claimed that that territory was theirs, and the Blackfoot-Kootenai never dared to hunt there again.
